text: The book describes the “container view,” on which time is a medium that would still exist and flow even if no events occurred. Whose account of time does it give as the paradigm of this view?
choices: Leibniz's, on which time is nothing but the network of relations among events
McTaggart's, on which the A-series is more fundamental than the B-series
Newton's absolute time, which “flows equably without relation to anything external”
Husserl's, on which time is constituted through retention and protention
explanation: The book names Newton's absolute time — which 'flows equably without relation to anything external' — as the paradigm container (absolute) view. Leibniz is offered as the paradigm of the opposing relational view, while McTaggart's A/B-series and Husserl's retention/protention belong to different debates in the unit.
